name: BodyTite

lead: BodyTite is a radiofrequency-assisted liposuction system from InMode. It removes fat and uses heat in the tissue to encourage the skin to tighten, aimed at patients who have loose skin that liposuction alone may not address.
Published work consists mostly of surgeon-authored series and retrospective reviews, with small registered studies.

paras: A subdermal probe delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy that liquefies fat and heats surrounding tissue, with temperature monitoring; the fat is then aspirated.

Reported effects include swelling, bruising and numbness, with burns, infection, seroma, hematoma and asymmetry described as less common. A 97-patient series reported major complications in 6.25% of patients per one summary. US clearance covers electrocoagulation and hemostasis.

trials.title: Retrospective Evaluation of Cellulite of Laxity Treatment Using Body Tite

lead: BodyTite is a radiofrequency-assisted liposuction (RFAL) system made by InMode. A probe placed beneath the skin delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy to liquefy fat and heat the tissue, after which the fat is aspirated; the heating is intended to make the skin contract, addressing laxity that liposuction alone may leave.[1][2]

It is used for body areas such as the abdomen, flanks, arms and thighs, and published reports describe it as filling a treatment gap between liposuction and excisional surgery such as brachioplasty or abdominoplasty.[3][4] Evidence consists mainly of surgeon-authored case series and retrospective reviews, with a small number of registered studies.

According to Grokipedia, the InMode RF System received US FDA 510(k) clearance (K163190) in December 2016 for electrocoagulation and hemostasis in dermatological and general surgical procedures, rather than for body contouring as such.[1]

paras: A 2018 supplement describes RFAL as a relatively new energy-assisted body contouring concept, using the BodyTite device to apply electromagnetic energy to soft tissue during suction lipectomy to produce soft tissue contraction.[3] Per Grokipedia, bipolar energy flows between an internal electrode in the cannula and an external electrode on the skin, with temperature and impedance monitoring intended to limit thermal injury.[1]

Reports describe use on the upper arms, where adding RFAL to liposuction was proposed to induce skin contraction in patients who might otherwise be recommended brachioplasty, with its visible scar.[5][6][4] A 2019 paper combined adjustable-depth fractional radiofrequency with bipolar radiofrequency for skin laxity in patients described as lying in a treatment gap.[7] A 2025 paper reports endotissutal bipolar radiofrequency for facial changes associated with weight-loss medication, sometimes called Ozempic face.[8]

A 2010 safety and feasibility study evaluated a novel radiofrequency-assisted liposuction technique.[9] A 2012 prospective series reported 97 patients treated under local anesthesia, at a time when the device was described as awaiting FDA approval,[2] and another 2012 series treated overweight patients for reshaping and tightening.[10] A 2012 upper-arm report described adding RFAL to liposuction.[5]

A 2023 report described BodyTite for upper arm lifting,[6] and a 2022 review covers nonexcisional arm contouring.[4] A 2024 retrospective review compared Renuvion helium plasma radiofrequency with BodyTite bipolar radiofrequency after liposuction or body contouring.[11] A registered retrospective evaluation of 10 participants examined treatment of cellulite of laxity.[12] Grokipedia summarises figures from some of these reports, including major complications in 6.25% and minor complications in 8.3% of the 97-patient series.[1] Studies are generally small and largely surgeon-authored.

Grokipedia lists swelling, bruising, numbness and tenderness as common effects, and burns, infection, seroma, hematoma and asymmetry as less common. It also states that FDA adverse event reports cite isolated cases of third-degree burns and cellulitis, and lists pregnancy, active infection and implanted electronic devices as contraindications.[1] Grokipedia itself notes that much of its sourcing is clinic marketing, so its statements are not independently verified here.

InMode, founded in 2008 by Moshe Mizrahy and Dr Michael Kreindel according to Grokipedia, developed the platform, with Dr Stephen Mulholland associated with early RFAL work.[1] The RF System obtained FDA clearance in December 2016, and a 40W configuration (K171593) followed in 2017, per the same source.[1] Smaller-area siblings include AccuTite and FaceTite.[13]

timeline.event: Safety and feasibility study of RFAL published.[9]
Series of 97 patients under local anesthesia published; device described as awaiting FDA approval.[2]
InMode RF System receives FDA 510(k) clearance K163190 (December).[1]
Supplement reviewing RFAL soft tissue contraction published.[3]
